hook.line: You have just heard something, and you want to check you got the point: "So you're telling me...". Tomás needs this one every time Hernando hints at something instead of saying it.
hook.es: O sea que el café no cierra.

examples.en: So you're not coming, then. (to a friend)

examples.es: O sea que todo fue culpa mía, ¿no?
examples.en: So it was all my fault, wasn't it?

examples.es: ¿O sea que Altamira ya compró el edificio?
examples.en: So Altamira has already bought the building?

examples.es: O sea que Tomás se queda.
No es tímido; mejor dicho, es reservado.
examples.en: He isn't shy; or rather, he's reserved.

examples.es: ¿O sea que usted no sabía nada?
examples.en: So you knew nothing? (to a stranger, formal)

rule:
*O sea que* + a full sentence says: "so what you mean is...". You pull the conclusion out of what the other person said and put it on the table. With a question mark, or a closing *¿no?*, it asks them to confirm. Without one, it can sound pointed.

*Mejor dicho* is a different job. It corrects yourself: the new words replace the old. *Es tímido; mejor dicho, es reservado.*

Both start a clause, with a comma after *mejor dicho*. Note the *que* in *o sea que*: no *que*, no conclusion.
smallPrint: Teachers call *o sea que* a consecutive reformulator, because it draws a consequence, and *mejor dicho* a rectifying one.

options: So you're not coming, then. (to a friend)
So I'm not coming.
So you came.

readAndPick.es: O sea que todo fue culpa mía, ¿no?
options: So it was all your fault, wasn't it?
So it was all my fault, wasn't it?
So it will all be my fault, won't it?

readAndPick.es: ¿O sea que Altamira ya compró el edificio?
options: Altamira wants to buy the building.
Altamira will buy the building.
So Altamira has already bought the building?

readAndPick.es: O sea que Tomás se queda.
options: So Tomás is staying.
So Tomás is leaving.
So Tomás stayed.

readAndPick.es: No es tímido; mejor dicho, es reservado.
options: He isn't shy; so he's reserved.
He isn't shy; or rather, he's reserved.
He isn't shy; for example, he's reserved.

readAndPick.es: ¿O sea que usted no sabía nada?
options: So you knew nothing? (to a stranger, formal)
So you know nothing? (to a friend)
So he knew nothing?

readAndPick.es: Vale dijo que viene. O sea que hay pastel.
options: Vale said she's coming. Or rather, there's cake.
Vale said she's coming. So there's cake.
Vale said she's coming, but there's no cake.

readAndPick.es: Hay tres ofertas, mejor dicho, dos.
options: There are three offers, so two.
There are three offers; there are also two.
There are three offers; or rather, two.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *O sea que* or *Mejor dicho* and type the whole sentence, drawing a conclusion: *___ el café no cierra.*
yourTurn.answer: O sea que el café no cierra.
yourTurn.why: You are concluding from what you heard, so *o sea que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say to a friend: So you're not coming, then.
yourTurn.why: *O sea que* plus the conclusion. A friend, so *vienes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask: So Altamira has already bought the building?
yourTurn.answer: ¿O sea que Altamira ya compró el edificio?
accept: ¿O sea que ya compró Altamira el edificio?
yourTurn.why: The same frame with question marks asks them to confirm.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: So it was all my fault, wasn't it?
yourTurn.answer: O sea que todo fue culpa mía, ¿no?
accept: ¿O sea que todo fue culpa mía?
yourTurn.why: The closing *¿no?* asks for agreement, like "wasn't it?".

yourTurn.prompt: Correct yourself: He isn't shy; or rather, he's reserved.
yourTurn.answer: No es tímido; mejor dicho, es reservado.
accept: No es tímido, mejor dicho, es reservado.
yourTurn.why: *Mejor dicho* replaces the first word with a better one.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a stranger, formally: So you knew nothing?
yourTurn.answer: ¿O sea que usted no sabía nada?
yourTurn.why: Same frame; *usted* and *sabía* keep it formal.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: *O sea que Tomás se queda.* (So Tomás isn't staying.)
yourTurn.answer: O sea que Tomás no se queda.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes right before *se queda*, just like in any other sentence.

pitfalls.right: O sea que Tomás se queda.
pitfalls.why: Almost. To draw a conclusion with a full sentence, *o sea* needs its *que*.

pitfalls.wrong: No es tímido; o sea que es reservado.
pitfalls.right: No es tímido; mejor dicho, es reservado.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *O sea que* draws a conclusion; to swap a word for a better one, use *mejor dicho*.

pitfalls.wrong: Hay tres ofertas, mejor dicho, hay tres ofertas.
pitfalls.right: Hay tres ofertas, mejor dicho, dos.
pitfalls.why: *Mejor dicho* has to bring a new version, or there is nothing to correct.

personal: Think of something a friend half-said lately. Write the conclusion you drew, starting with *O sea que...*, as if you were checking you understood.
